# Chemical Bonding

## Why Atoms Bond

Atoms bond to reach a more stable, lower-energy arrangement of electrons. Most atoms are most stable with eight electrons in their outer shell, which is called the octet rule. Hydrogen and helium are exceptions, being stable with two. You will need this rule for every topic that follows.

## Ionic Bonds

Ionic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. It forms when a metal transfers one or more electrons to a non-metal. Sodium chloride is the classic example: sodium gives one electron to chlorine, forming Na+ and Cl- ions. Ionic compounds have high melting points and conduct electricity when molten or dissolved, but not as solids. Their ions are held in a giant lattice.

## Covalent Bonds

A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms. Atoms can share one, two or three pairs, giving single, double and triple bonds. Triple bonds are shorter and stronger than single bonds. Simple covalent molecules such as water and carbon dioxide have low melting points, because only weak forces act between the molecules.

### Polarity

When two atoms with different electronegativities share electrons, the shared pair is pulled toward the more electronegative atom. This creates a polar bond with a partial negative charge on one end and a partial positive charge on the other. Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group. Fluorine has the highest value, 4.0 on the Pauling scale. A molecule with polar bonds can still be non-polar overall if its shape is symmetrical, as in carbon dioxide.

## Metallic Bonds

In a metal, the outer electrons leave their atoms and form a sea of delocalized electrons around a lattice of positive ions. This structure explains why metals conduct heat and electricity. Metals are malleable because layers of ions can slide over each other without breaking the bond. Copper is used for electrical wiring for exactly this reason.

## Intermolecular Forces

Intermolecular forces act between molecules and are much weaker than the bonds inside them. London dispersion forces exist between all molecules and grow stronger with more electrons. Dipole-dipole forces act between polar molecules. Hydrogen bonds form when hydrogen is bonded to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine, and they give water its unusually high boiling point of 100 °C. Students often confuse these forces with covalent bonds, so check your notes carefully.
